target.title: Install ClawHub packages for new Claw agents
target.body:
## Summary

- preflight each exact, version-pinned ClawHub package as install or reuse and bind that owner decision into the consented plan
- revalidate plugin owner state immediately before mutation, then use the existing skill and plugin installer surfaces
- persist pending, complete, or failed package provenance so partial installs and independently owned packages remain explainable
- return structured partial results when a package or later agent/config mutation fails after package work has begun
- warn across CLI, Gateway, and Control UI plugin removal when any Claw provenance, including uncertain provenance, references the plugin

## Scope

This is the package-owner slice of the experimental Claw lifecycle. It keeps the grouped RFC contract (`packages[].kind`, `source`, `ref`, and exact `version`) and deliberately does not restore generic artifact selectors or agent skill lists. MCP servers and cron jobs remain blocked for later stack slices.

The dry-run records whether each package is absent or already present at the exact version. Apply requires the matching plan digest and rechecks plugin owner state before invoking the installer, so a package cannot silently change from Claw-installed to independently owned, or the reverse, after consent. Package work runs before agent/config/workspace mutation; any later collision returns a partial result that retains the package evidence.

Package references describe dependency provenance, not exclusive ownership. An exact package reused from the operator is recorded as independently owned. A Claw-started install is recorded before external mutation and transitions from pending to complete or failed. Existing experimental databases receive the new update timestamp through an additive migration. Plugin uninstall remains operator-controlled but warns for complete and uncertain Claw references.

The CLI remains process-gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1` in the base of this stack.

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #101973 managed workspace files
- This PR: package owner preflight, installers, provenance, and shared uninstall warnings
- Next: #102296 status and remove

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:core`
- `pnpm tsgo:test:src`
- focused Oxlint on changed Claw, plugin, and state files
- 47 focused package, provenance, plugin-uninstall, and state-database tests
- 6 Claw lifecycle E2E tests
- `codex-review --mode local` clean after addressing additive migration, error preservation, and uncertain-reference warning findings

The embedded-agent runner reports useful startup milestones through an internal callback, but public diagnostic subscribers cannot currently observe them. ## Why This Change Was Made

Adds the public additive diagnostic event `run.execution_phase` with the existing run/session correlation fields and the runner's phase payload. Documentation explicitly treats diagnostic event kinds as additive and tells external consumers to keep a default branch rather than assume exhaustive event-kind handling.

Diagnostics consumers can now show meaningful turn-startup progress without subscribing to an internal control-UI path. Existing callbacks and consumers retain their behavior; diagnostics-disabled processes emit nothing.

target.title: [Bug]: gpt-5.3-codex-spark emits empty arguments for required tool calls
target.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark emitted structured OpenClaw tool calls with empty argument objects for tools that require arguments, causing schema validation to reject every call before execution.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an isolated OpenClaw subagent with:

  • Model: openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark
  • Runtime: agentRuntime.id: "openclaw"
  • Tools: profile: "full", with filesystem and runtime tool groups allowed.
2. Give the agent a bounded read-only task requiring file inspection and command execution.

3. Observe its tool calls and validation results.

### Expected behavior

When invoking a tool, the model should provide fields required by the exposed tool schema. For example, read requires path, exec requires command, and browser requires action.

### Actual behavior

The model emitted calls with empty arguments:

```
read({})
exec({})
browser({})
```

OpenClaw rejected them before execution:

```
Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}
```

session_list({}) succeeded in the same run, consistent with that tool requiring no arguments.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1

### Operating system

Linux 6.17.0-1018-oracle arm64

### Install method

docker

### Model

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw embedded runtime (agentRuntime.id: "openclaw") → OpenAI ChatGPT Responses transport → gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Additional provider/model setup details

• Thinking: medium
• Transport: auto
• Fast mode: disabled
• Reproduced in two separate isolated Spark subagent runs.
• The issue occurred before the affected agent was later changed to Luna.

### Logs

```shell
text

Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "exec":
  - command: must have required properties command

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "browser":
  - action: must have required properties action

Received arguments:
{}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: two isolated Spark subagent runs in one OpenClaw deployment.
Severity: high, because file reads, command execution, browser actions, and native-search workflows cannot proceed.
Frequency: observed in 2/2 Spark test runs.
Consequence: required-argument tools fail before execution.


### Additional information

This differs from the Kimi plain-text/XML tool-call issue in #40069. Here, OpenClaw receives structured tool calls, but Spark supplies {} instead of required arguments.

target.title: fix(line): dripping inbound media downloads hang past setup timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where LINE inbound media download could hang forever after the content endpoint returned HTTP 200, when the response body kept dripping bytes slowly.

Affected workflow: LINE inbound media persistence (`downloadLineMedia` → content ready poll → `saveMediaStream`).

## Why This Change Was Made

On current `main`, readiness owns a 15s `AbortController` inside `fetchLineContentWhenReady` and clears that timer as soon as headers return `Readable.fromWeb(response.body)`. After headers, only the Node stream remains — with no wall-clock — so a slow drip can keep `saveMediaStream` alive indefinitely.

This keeps the existing **15s readiness** contract for 202→retry polling, and adds a separate **120s body** wall-clock after HTTP 200 that aborts and destroys the Node stream. Body budget matches Slack/Feishu inbound media totals (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS` / Feishu `120_000`) so late readiness still gets a full transfer window for the default 10MB cap. LINE documents `api-data.line.me` as the large-data content endpoint where video/audio may spend time preparing before binary retrieval ([Get content](https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#get-content)).

Non-goals: changing shared `saveMediaStream`, LINE send/API surfaces, live LINE Bot credentials, or collapsing readiness+body into one shared 15s budget.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/line/src/download.ts` open PRs = 0 (all authors and Pick-cat).

## User Impact

- Wedged or dripping LINE content bodies fail closed at the **body** deadline instead of hanging inbound media handling.
- Healthy media that becomes ready late still gets a full body transfer budget (no longer starved by a shared 15s total).
- Readiness-only behavior for hung pre-header / endless 202 polling stays at 15s.

## Evidence

Exact head: `7f923be17856f009af73fc12858463fa97bcfd3f`.

### Timeout contract (post-fix)

| Phase | Budget | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Readiness | `CONTENT_READY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 15s | 202 polling until HTTP 200 headers |
| Body | `LINE_MEDIA_BODY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s | `saveMediaStream` after headers; stream destroyed on abort |

Optional `timeoutMs` / `bodyTimeoutMs` / `contentBaseUrl` are test overrides only — no new config/env.

### Observed real-behavior proof (local Vitest + `node:http` loopback)

Command:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/line/src/download.test.ts extensions/line/src/download.deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

Result at this head:

```text
✓ aborts a dripping content body within the body wall-clock deadline 474ms
✓ persists a slow-but-valid body before the body deadline 89ms
✓ aborts a hung content request at the readiness deadline 5ms
✓ aborts a dripping content body after headers within the body deadline 54ms
✓ keeps a fresh body deadline after late readiness 1ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 4.83s
```

Concrete contract observations (not just green checks):

- **Body drip fail-closed:** real `node:http` peer returns HTTP 200 then drips 1 byte every 40ms; with `bodyTimeoutMs: 250`, rejection is `LINE media body for message mid-drip timed out after 0.25 seconds`, and wall-clock elapsed lands in `[200, 2000)` (observed ~474ms — bounded, not an indefinite hang).
- **Slow-but-valid success:** same loopback path with an 80ms paced body and `bodyTimeoutMs: 1500` completes (`size: 2`, observed ~89ms) — healthy slow transfer is not false-killed.
- **Readiness unchanged:** hung pre-header fetch still rejects with `did not become ready within 15 seconds`; readiness `AbortSignal` aborts; `saveMediaStream` is not called.
- **Separate budgets:** drip-after-headers abort uses the **body** error string while the readiness signal stays un-aborted; late readiness (~14s 202 hang) + 1.5s slow-valid body still succeeds under a fresh 2s body budget (would fail a shared 15s total).
- Sibling contracts checked: `extensions/slack/src/monitor/media.ts` (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000`), Feishu media HTTP 120s, LINE Get content large-data prep notes.
- What was not tested: live `api-data.line.me` with channel credentials (no live LINE bot in this contributor environment). Controlled local drip + slow-valid + readiness hang cover the changed fail-closed contract.

### Verification

- `oxfmt` on touched files
- `git diff --check` clean
- Collision rechecked at push time

### Risk / Compatibility

Readiness semantics unchanged (15s). Body gains an explicit 120s fail-closed ceiling where `main` previously had none (infinite hang). No new config keys. AI-assisted.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Vydra image/audio/video generation could hang forever when a CDN returned response headers and then dripped the body slowly enough to keep resetting the per-chunk idle timer. `fetchWithTimeout` clears its abort after headers land, so the download budget no longer applied to the body — including non-2xx error-detail reads.

## Why This Change Was Made

At the `downloadVydraAsset` call site only, keep one wall-clock deadline across headers + non-2xx error-detail + successful-body reads via `readResponseTextPrefix` / `readResponseWithLimit({ timeoutMs, onTimeout })`, matching Discord `probe.ts` / `readDiscordProbeGetMeJson`.

Shared `fetchWithTimeout` and `assertOkOrThrowHttpError` are intentionally unchanged (the shared assert helper has no wall-clock body budget).

Collision check: searched open/closed PRs for `downloadVydraAsset` / Vydra drip wall-clock; no competing open PR. Related hang-class siblings (Discord probe / ClawHub body deadline) are separate owners.

## User Impact

Vydra media downloads fail within the configured HTTP timeout when a remote body keeps trickling instead of completing — for both 2xx asset bodies and dripping non-2xx error bodies. Generation no longer sticks forever on a slow-drip CDN response.

## Evidence

Exact head: `391009428f4a6506d45aa404ca35f0f016859ff5`

```bash
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/vydra/shared.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

target.title: fix(clawhub): keep request deadline through response body
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ClawHub registry requests could hang past their configured deadline when response headers arrived but the body stalled or dripped slowly. `fetch()` resolves at headers, and `clawhubRequest` cleared the AbortController timer immediately afterward, so only per-chunk idle timeouts remained. A continuous drip that resets chunk-idle could exceed the intended total budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the same request AbortSignal deadline active through body consumption for every ClawHub caller. `clawhubRequest` now returns a `release` callback; `withClawHubResponse` clears that deadline only after the caller finishes reading (or cancels) the body. Retries release abandoned attempts before the next try. No new config or public API surface.

Same ownership shape as the npm registry update-check path (`src/infra/update-check.ts`) and the Discord webhook timeout fix (#109076).

Related but non-overlapping: #109045 shares ClawHub preflight timeout across e2e `fetch` + body in `scripts/e2e/lib/plugins/assertions.mjs` only — it does not touch `src/infra/clawhub.ts`.

## User Impact

ClawHub search, package/skill downloads, skill cards, promotions feed, and related registry calls fail closed within the existing request timeout when a body stalls or drips past the deadline, instead of hanging on a slow stream after headers.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

ClawHub request timeout covers headers **and** body. Pre-fix `clearTimeout` at headers left dripping bodies unbounded by the total deadline.

### Canonical reachability path

`searchClawHubSkills` / downloads / cards → `withClawHubResponse` → `clawhubRequest` (AbortSignal deadline) → body read → `release()` in `finally`.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/clawhub.test.ts --reporter=dot
```

Result: `Test Files  1 passed (1)` / `Tests  82 passed | 2 skipped (84)` in ~4.2s.

New coverage:
- keeps the request deadline through stalled bodies after headers (signal-linked stream)
- aborts JSON bodies that drip past the request deadline (chunk-idle alone insufficient)
- negative control: clearing the deadline at headers leaves a drip unbounded

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node `v22.22.0`, standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only, native `fetch` + the post-fix deadline ownership (release after body):

- **Stalled body:** incomplete JSON after headers aborted with `ClawHub request timed out after 250ms` at **252 ms** under a 250 ms deadline → `PASS`
- **Normal body:** HTTP 200 JSON completed in **5 ms** under a 1 s deadline → `PASS`
- **Negative control:** early `clearTimeout` at headers + continuous drip; after **600 ms** body still unsettled and signal not aborted → `PASS`

Summary: `{\"stall\":\"PASS\",\"normal\":\"PASS\",\"negative\":\"PASS\"}`

### Diff hygiene

- Head: `7a52a04622b350337322d7e0fac592ae35b86567`
- `git diff --check` clean
- Touched: `src/infra/clawhub.ts`, `src/infra/clawhub.test.ts`

### What was not tested

Live ClawHub registry against `https://clawhub.ai` (no credentials / no external network in this proof).

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the deadline ownership, every `clawhubRequest` caller migration through `withClawHubResponse`, retry `disposeRetry` release, regression tests (including negative control), and loopback proof before opening this PR.

target.title: fix(agents): dripping proxy SSE bodies cancel via outer abort
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes concern that an OpenClaw proxy LLM SSE body can keep dripping after headers and reset per-chunk idle forever. Total stream lifetime must stay owned by the configured outer agent/provider abort budget (`signal`), not a hidden proxy-local ceiling.

Affected workflow: `streamProxy` (`/api/stream` SSE) when agents route model calls through a proxy server.

## Why This Change Was Made

`streamProxy` already bounds pre-header waits and per-chunk SSE idle (default 120s). After headers, the pre-header abort is intentionally cleared so `timeoutMs` is not an absolute stream deadline (#97235). Idle alone resets on every chunk.

ClawSweeper rejected an unconditional one-hour proxy-local default (`merge-risk: compatibility`) because whole-run budgets can exceed 1h. This revision:

1. Keeps total lifetime owned by `options.signal` / outer abort by default — **no proxy-local default ceiling**.
2. Keeps `streamDeadlineMs` as an **opt-in only** escape hatch for callers who explicitly want a proxy-local wall-clock.
3. Arms that opt-in deadline only after the response reader exists so `cancel()` can interrupt a drip.
4. Adds native loopback `/api/stream` proof for both outer abort and explicit `streamDeadlineMs`.

Non-goals: making pre-header `timeoutMs` an absolute stream deadline again; documenting a new one-hour product contract; live proxy provider auth.

## User Impact

Dripping keepalive-style proxy SSE bodies are canceled when the outer abort fires, without cutting off healthy streams that are still within a longer configured agent/provider budget. Callers that explicitly pass `streamDeadlineMs` get a bounded proxy-local wall-clock; everyone else keeps the prior lifetime ownership model.

boot-time codex auto-enable for OAuth-gated models, or skips
re-resolving models whose configuration did not change.

target.title: Feature request: opt-in (or disable-able) agent-to-agent "announce step"
target.body:
# Feature request: opt-in (or disable-able) agent-to-agent "announce step"

**Version:** 2026.6.11 (e085fa1)

## Summary

Cross-agent `sessions_send` (and subagent completion delivery) runs a second, hidden **announce step** in the *target* agent's session. This step is **opt-out**: whatever the target model emits is posted to the target agent's human channel **unless** the reply is exactly the `ANNOUNCE_SKIP` sentinel. There is no config surface to suppress or make this opt-in — `tools.agentToAgent` exposes only `enabled` and `allow`.

The result is a footgun: any target agent that fails to emit the exact sentinel leaks an unintended message to *its own human*. This is fine for models that reliably follow the sentinel instruction, but it makes safe cross-agent messaging depend on model discipline rather than on configuration.

## Current behavior (from source)

- `sessions_send` into agent B's `:main` session is two turns:
  1. B processes the message → reply returns to the **caller** only.
  2. OpenClaw runs a hidden **announce step** in B's session (`subagent-session-cleanup` / `openclaw-tools`), prompting B to optionally message its own human. Per `docs/tools/subagents.md`: *"then runs an announce step and posts the announce reply to the requester."*
- Suppression is exact-sentinel only: `isAnnounceSkip(text)` requires the reply to normalize to `ANNOUNCE_SKIP`. Any other text (e.g. a stray status line like `"Relayed to Esther 🥊"`) is delivered to B's human.
- `tools.agentToAgent` schema (runtime-schema) has exactly two keys: `enabled`, `allow`. No `announce` / `announceMode` control exists.

## Why this is a problem

The announce step is **post-by-default**. Safety-by-construction would be **silent-by-default**: an agent should have to *deliberately* choose to notify its human (e.g. by calling a `notify_human` tool), not be relied upon to type an exact opt-out token every time. Weaker/cheaper models (we pin two nudge-heavy agents to Gemini 3 Flash for cost/latency) do not reliably emit the sentinel — especially on the "push relay" branch — and leak a spurious message to the target's human on every miss.

Today the only ways to prevent the leak are:
1. **Prompt-level** — instruct the agent to emit `ANNOUNCE_SKIP` (model-dependent, unreliable on smaller models), or
2. **Transport-level** — remove the agents from `tools.agentToAgent.allow` entirely, which also kills *legitimate* inbound messaging to them (both ends are gated by `matchesAllow(requester) && matchesAllow(target)`).

There is no middle option: "allow messaging, but don't auto-announce to the human."

## Proposed fix (any one of these would close the gap)

1. **Config toggle** on `tools.agentToAgent` (and the subagent completion path): `announce: "auto" | "off" | "optIn"`, ideally also settable **per-agent** (`agents.list[].announce`). `off` = never run the announce step; the caller reply is the only delivery.
2. **Opt-in model:** replace the opt-out sentinel with an explicit `notify_human` tool the target must call to reach its human; default is silent.
3. **Minimal version:** honor a per-agent flag that skips the announce step entirely for that agent.

Option 1 (`announce: "off"`, per-agent) is the smallest change that fully removes the footgun without touching the messaging allowlist, and it benefits any deployment mixing model tiers across agents.

## Impact

Affects anyone running cross-agent orchestration where a target agent runs a model that doesn't perfectly follow the exact-sentinel instruction. The leak is silent (posts to a real human channel) and only discoverable by the human noticing an unexpected message.

target.title: Model fallback skips OpenAI provider cooldown even when another auth profile is healthy
target.body:
## Summary

In a multi-auth-profile OpenAI setup, model fallback skipped the entire `openai` provider as cooldowned even though a separate OpenAI auth profile had just been selected as healthy by the quota sampler. This caused a new embedded agent run to fail over to Google/Gemini and then report "all models temporarily rate-limited", without attempting the healthy OpenAI profile.

All account identifiers, emails, chat IDs, and message IDs below are redacted.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.6.10` (`aa69b12` reported by `/status`)
- Local upstream checkout: `openclaw/openclaw@61c27c3187cc5b5b5962914eb6279fe38f937c2a`
- Runtime: embedded agent / Telegram route
- Model chain: primary `openai/gpt-5.5`, fallback `google/gemini-3.5-flash`
- Auth setup: multiple `openai` OAuth profiles

## Expected behavior

If at least one auth profile for a provider is eligible and not in cooldown/disabled state, model fallback should not skip the entire provider. It should attempt the healthy profile, or at minimum run the profile-aware cooldown probe path before falling through to a different provider.

A limited profile should not poison the whole provider when another profile is healthy.

## Actual behavior

After the quota sampler had selected a healthy OpenAI profile, a fresh/new embedded agent run skipped `openai/gpt-5.5` with:

```text
model fallback decision: decision=skip_candidate requested=openai/gpt-5.5 candidate=openai/gpt-5.5 reason=rate_limit next=google/gemini-3.5-flash detail=Provider openai is in cooldown (suspending lanes)
```

It then tried `google/gemini-3.5-flash`, which returned quota exhausted, so the user-visible result was an all-models rate-limit failure.

## Timeline / Evidence

Quota sampler evidence, sanitized:

```jsonl
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:15:26.374Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:20:41.365Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":true,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:25:48.857Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:30:39.071Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:35:24.884Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
```

Fallback evidence, sanitized:

```text
2026-07-12T12:34:22.697Z [model-fallback/decision]
model fallback decision: decision=skip_candidate requested=openai/gpt-5.5 candidate=openai/gpt-5.5 reason=rate_limit next=google/gemini-3.5-flash detail=Provider openai is in cooldown (suspending lanes)

2026-07-12T12:34:23.579Z [telegram]
embedded run agent end: isError=true model=gemini-3.5-flash provider=google error=Google Generative AI API error (429) ... [code=RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED]

2026-07-12T12:34:23.712Z
Embedded agent failed before reply: All models failed (2): openai/gpt-5.5: Provider openai is in cooldown (suspending lanes) (rate_limit) | google/gemini-3.5-flash: Google Generative AI API error (429) ... [code=RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED]
```

Current auth profile state, sanitized, shows only the limited profile had cooldown/disabled fields; the healthy profile did not:

```json
{
  "order": {
    "openai": ["openai:<healthy-profile>"]
  },
  "lastGood": {
    "openai": "openai:<healthy-profile>"
  },
  "usageStats": {
    "openai:<healthy-profile>": {
      "errorCount": 0
    },
    "openai:<limited-profile>": {
      "blockedReason": "subscription_limit",
      "cooldownReason": "rate_limit",
      "cooldownModel": "gpt-5.5",
      "failureCounts": { "rate_limit": 2, "quota": 1 },
      "disabledReason": "quota"
    }
  }
}
```

## Impact

- New sessions can still fail even after account balancing selects a healthy OpenAI profile.
- The user-visible error claims all models are temporarily rate-limited, but a healthy same-provider profile was known from quota sampling.
- Multi-account rotation loses its recovery value when provider-level cooldown/suspension overrides profile-level health.

## Suspected area

Likely in model fallback / embedded runner auth profile selection interaction:

- `src/agents/model-fallback.ts`
- `src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run.ts`
- `src/agents/auth-profiles/order.ts`
- `src/agents/auth-profiles/usage.ts`

The important invariant seems to be: provider-level cooldown skip should only happen when all eligible profiles for that provider are actually unavailable in the same auth store/order view used by the embedded runner.

## Suggested fix direction

Before returning provider-level `skip_candidate` for cooldown/rate-limit, re-check whether the provider has any eligible non-cooldown profile. If it does, attempt that profile instead of skipping the provider. If an external quota sampler has marked a profile healthy, the fallback path should not emit "all models failed" until that profile has been attempted or explicitly rejected by the same runtime path.

### Summary

In the main assistant session, both `exec` and `read` tools frequently return empty output. Simple commands like `echo hello world` and `whoami` return nothing. Reading existing files (e.g. `SOUL.md`, `BUG-REPORT.md`) returns empty. The bug is intermittent and session-specific: sub-agents spawned from the same host work correctly, and `host="gateway"` sometimes briefly restores output.

### Affected docs path(s) or URL(s)

n/a

### Steps to reproduce / verify

1. Start OpenClaw on Windows 11 with 2026.6.10/11.
2. In the main session, run `exec` with `echo hello world`.
3. Observe empty output.
4. Run `read` on any existing file (e.g. `SOUL.md`).
5. Observe empty output.
6. Try `host="gateway"` — output may return briefly, then fail again.
7. Spawn a sub-agent via `sessions_spawn` and run the same command — output works correctly.


### Expected docs behavior/content

- `exec echo hello world` should return `hello world`.
- `read SOUL.md` should return the file contents.



### Actual docs behavior/content

- Both return empty strings.
- No error message is shown.
- The failure is silent.


### Impact

- `memory_search` and other non-exec/read tools continue working.

### Evidence

- `memory_search` and other non-exec/read tools continue working.

target.title: [Bug] Destructive Formatting in sanitizeForPromptLiteral Strips Tabs and Newlines
target.body:
### Summary / Problem Statement
In `src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts`, `sanitizeForPromptLiteral` uses a broad regular expression to match Unicode control characters (`Cc`). This regex inadvertently strips tabs (`\t`) and newlines (`\n`), destroying code indentation and layout alignment before forwarding the payload to the LLM.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Vulnerable Code Location:** [src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts#L19)
- **Mechanics:**
  ```typescript
  const CcPattern = /[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\u2028\u2029]/gu;
  return input.replace(CcPattern, "");
  ```
- The category `\p{Cc}` matches all control characters, including tabs and newlines, destroying code block structure.

### Impact Analysis
- Loss of code indentation in prompt injections, causing degraded LLM code understanding.
- Failure of code-related operations (like syntax analysis) that depend on correct indentation.

### Proposed Solution
1. Exclude tab (`\u0009`) and newline (`\u000A`, `\u000D`) characters from the sanitization pattern.

### Affected File References
- [sanitize-for-prompt.ts:L10-L25](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts#L10-L25)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Critical Quality `network-runtime-boundary` fails closed on current `main` whenever a PR touches `extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.ts` (or otherwise triggers the full raw-socket CodeQL shard), because `openApnsTlsTunnel` performs a managed `tls.connect` that is not classified in the owner allowlist.

## Why This Change Was Made

The proxy CONNECT refactor extracted APNs target TLS into `openApnsTlsTunnel`, but the raw-socket CodeQL allowlist still only named the outer `openProxiedApnsHttp2Session` / `connectApnsHttp2Session` scopes. CodeQL attributes the call to the immediate enclosing function (`openApnsTlsTunnel`), so the existing outer-function entries do not cover it.

This PR only restores the missing owner classification for that already-shipped managed APNs tunnel callsite. No runtime behavior change.

Collision check: searched open/closed PRs for `openApnsTlsTunnel` allowlist; only overlapping work was bundled inside [#106519](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/106519), which ClawSweeper asked to split. This is that separated security-boundary unit.

## User Impact

- **Before:** Unrelated Codex/network PRs that trigger the full network-runtime CodeQL shard can fail on an unclassified APNs `tls.connect` that already exists on `main`.
- **After:** The managed APNs TLS tunnel owner is classified, so the shard can evaluate new raw-socket calls without failing on this pre-existing callsite.

target.title: fix(ollama): dripping model pulls hang past idle timeout during setup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw Ollama setup could hang forever while downloading a model when `/api/pull` kept sending occasional NDJSON progress lines that never advanced `completed`.

Affected workflow: Ollama provider setup / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` model download.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ollama setup already aborts if headers never arrive (30s) and already fails if the pull stream goes fully idle (300s). After headers return, that response timer was cleared, so only the per-chunk idle timer remained. Idle resets on every chunk, so a slow drip can keep the download alive indefinitely.

This keeps the headers and byte-idle budgets as-is, then arms a **no-progress watchdog** after the first body chunk. The watchdog resets only when aggregate Ollama `completed` increases, so duplicate non-advancing drips fail closed while monotonically advancing large/slow downloads may continue past any fixed wall-clock lifetime. Optional `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs` / `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `ensureOllamaModelPulled` are for tests only — no new config key or env var. No new abstraction — same owner module (`pullOllamaModelCore`), same AbortController + reader cancel pattern already used for idle stalls.

ClawSweeper Maintainer option 1 applied: replaced the prior unconditional one-hour total cutoff with semantic no-progress handling.

Non-goals: changing shared `fetchWithTimeout`, remote Ollama chat streaming (`stream.ts`), or adding a hard total lifetime cap.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` open PRs = 0 for this timeout policy. Nearby open ollama PRs touch streaming/NDJSON elsewhere, not setup pull no-progress.

## User Impact

During Ollama setup, a wedged or maliciously dripping `/api/pull` stream (bytes without advancing `completed`) fails closed with a no-progress error instead of hanging the wizard forever. Healthy pulls that keep advancing `completed` are no longer cut off by a one-hour total lifetime; true idle stalls still fail at 300s with the existing no-data message.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

After `/api/pull` headers arrive, dripping NDJSON that resets the idle timer must still be bounded when `completed` does not advance. Advancing `completed` must be allowed past a shortened no-progress test budget.

### Canonical reachability path

Setup wizard / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` → `pullOllamaModel` → `pullOllamaModelCore` → first body chunk arms no-progress → advancing `completed` re-arms → non-advancing drip → `reader.cancel()` → no-progress error → `WizardCancelledError`.

### Focused tests

Exact head: `bf6b4987916837b2712d510ff2ef382736331edb`

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  34 passed (34)
```

Coverage:
- existing idle-stall regression still green at 300s with **no data** message (empty body; no-progress not armed)
- fake-timer non-advancing drip (`streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 1000`, idle 10s) fails with no-progress message
- fake-timer advancing `completed` continues past several shortened no-progress windows and downloads successfully
- loopback negative control: drip every 40ms + idle 100ms stays unsettled at 500ms (idle alone insufficient)
- loopback positive control: non-advancing drip + `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` rejects with no-progress message
- loopback advancing control: `completed` advances every 80ms under `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` and finishes successfully past that budget

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node local Vitest + standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only:

- **Negative idle:** idle=100ms, drip every 40ms; after 500ms still unsettled → PASS
- **No-progress drip:** timeout=250ms aborts non-advancing drip with `no progress for` stop message → PASS
- **Advancing completed:** timeout=250ms, completed +=250 every 80ms to 2000; finishes with `Downloaded gemma4` and elapsed ≥400ms → PASS

### Diff hygiene

- Exact head: `bf6b4987916837b2712d510ff2ef382736331edb`
- Rebased onto current `origin/main`
- `oxfmt` on touched files; `git diff --check` clean
- Touched: `extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts`, `setup.test.ts`, `setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts`

### What was not tested

Live `ollama.com` / LAN Ollama daemon multi-hour large-model pull; controlled local drip + advancing `completed` only.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

### Risk / Compatibility

Low. Removes the previous unconditional one-hour total cutoff (compatibility-preserving vs that draft). Retains headers + byte-idle. Adds semantic no-progress aligned with idle budget (300s default). Test-only timeout overrides only (no new config/env). Intentional fail-closed for indefinitely non-advancing drips.

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the idle-vs-no-progress contract, first-chunk arming so empty stalls keep the no-data message, `completed`-only reset, advancing-progress regressions, loopback negative/positive/advancing controls, and proof before refresh.

target.title: fix(plugins): plugins.deny is bypassed by a mixed-case manifest id
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who denylist a plugin would still have that plugin load in full, when the plugin's manifest declares its id in a different case than the denylist entry.

Plugin config policy lists are lowercase-normalized: `plugins.deny`, `plugins.allow`, and `plugins.entries` keys all pass through `normalizePluginId`, which trims and lowercases. A plugin's self-declared manifest id is only trimmed. So when an operator denylists `malicious-scraper` and a plugin publishes `"id": "Malicious-Scraper"`, the denylist comparison misses, no diagnostic is emitted, and the plugin falls through to default activation with its hooks, channels, secret provider integrations, and tools loaded. The operator sees the plugin listed as enabled with no indication their denylist entry did nothing.

The same gap applies to the core reserved-id check: a manifest declaring `"id": "Node-MCP"` evades the `CORE_RESERVED_PLUGIN_IDS` rejection that `node-mcp` would hit.

The allowlist side of the mismatch fails closed rather than open: a legitimately allowlisted plugin that declares a mixed-case id is blocked as `not-in-allowlist`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/plugins/manifest.ts:1787` mints `PluginManifestRecord.id`, the value every downstream policy consumer compares against config:

```ts
// before
const id = normalizeOptionalString(raw.id) ?? "";
```

`normalizeOptionalString` trims only, while `src/plugins/config-state.ts` normalizes every config-side id with `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString`. The two sides of each comparison are in different cases. The consumers that mismatch:

- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts:57` - `normalizedConfig.deny.includes(params.plugin.id)`
- `src/plugins/config-activation-shared.ts:161` - `params.config.deny.includes(params.id)`

The fix canonicalizes at the parse boundary:

```ts
// after
const id = normalizeOptionalLowercaseString(raw.id) ?? "";
```

`manifest.ts` is the single point where a manifest id becomes a `PluginManifestRecord.id`, and `manifest-registry.ts` builds every record's `id` from that value. Canonicalizing here fixes the denylist check, the allowlist check, the per-entry `enabled: false` check, and the reserved-id check at once, rather than patching each comparison site and leaving the next one to re-introduce the gap. `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString` is the same trim-plus-lowercase helper the config side already uses.

Alias mapping deliberately stays out of the manifest path. `normalizePluginId` also resolves legacy config aliases, which is an input-normalization concern for operator-typed config, not for a manifest declaring its own identity.

Sibling manifest-id readers checked and unaffected:

- `src/plugins/manifest-metadata-scan.ts:197` uses a trimmed id purely as a local dedupe/ranking key within the scan, comparing raw ids to raw ids. It never reaches allow/deny policy.
- `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-record-reader.ts:88` builds install-index records describing which packages are installed. Activation policy keys off `loadPluginManifest`, not this record.

Related but distinct: closed PR #59595 patched the same raw-vs-normalized class of mismatch at the `warnAboutUntrackedLoadedPlugins()` call site in `loader.ts`, for aliases, affecting a provenance warning. This change fixes the security-relevant deny/activation path at its source.

## User Impact

Operators who denylist a plugin now have that denylist honored regardless of the case the plugin author chose for its manifest id. A plugin can no longer self-select out of `plugins.deny` by publishing a mixed-case id, and cannot claim a mixed-case spelling of a core reserved id.

All 59 manifest ids shipped in this repo are already lowercase, so canonicalization is a no-op for every bundled plugin. Config-side behavior is untouched. Operators who had worked around the bug by adding a mixed-case denylist entry are unaffected, since config-side entries were already lowercased before comparison.

## Evidence

### Redacted live Gateway runtime inspection

A new integration fixture starts the real Gateway plugin bootstrap path through `loadPluginLookUpTable()` and `loadGatewayStartupPlugins()` with two on-disk bundled plugins:

- Denied manifest ID: `Denied-Fixture`; canonical runtime export ID: `denied-fixture`
- Allowed manifest ID: `Allowed-Fixture`; canonical runtime export ID: `allowed-fixture`
- Config: `allow: ["allowed-fixture"]`, `deny: ["denied-fixture"]`

Both fixtures attempt to register a legacy hook, typed Gateway hook, tool, channel, service, and secret-provider integration. The allowed fixture deliberately exports the canonical lowercase ID, exercising the loader's exact manifest/runtime ID contract.

The Gateway registry inspection asserts this redacted snapshot:

```json
{
  "deniedRegistryRecord": null,
  "imported": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "hooks": ["allowed-fixture", "allowed-fixture"],
  "tools": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "channels": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "services": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "secretIntegrations": ["allowed-fixture"]
}
```

This proves the denied mixed-case plugin is rejected before runtime registration: it has no registry record and contributes no imported runtime, hook, tool, channel, service, or secret-integration surface. The allowed mixed-case manifest loads successfully under the canonical `allowed-fixture` identity across every inspected surface.

Implementation: `src/gateway/server-plugin-bootstrap.browser-plugin.integration.test.ts`.

### Cold CLI-path regression context

The earlier on-disk CLI-path reproduction remains useful as the before/after activation check:

```text
# BEFORE (pristine main a8fe7dd834)
plugin id="Malicious-Scraper" enabled=true status="loaded"
# AFTER (patched tree, identical inputs)
plugin id="malicious-scraper" enabled=false status="disabled"
```

### Validation and branch status

- Rebased onto current `main` at `a327e43023cb9aa2e77162fc40a604655aa83557`.
- Current head: `3ca2ea71a40efad290cb1617bd6b6127326c184c`.
- Autoreview: clean; no actionable findings.
- The refreshed CI already cleared the original branch failures in `check-test-types` and `checks-node-compact-small-3` on the first refreshed head.
- `checks-node-compact-small-11` passed with the corrected live Gateway inspection: 128 Gateway-shard tests passed, including the denied/allowed surface proof.

Unit coverage also verifies lowercase identity, deny blocking, allow activation, disabled entries, reserved IDs, and unchanged lowercase IDs. The original manifest suite passed 132 focused assertions on Node 24 before the Gateway proof was added.

- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.

## Linked context

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text

- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:


target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
